title: Cloud Providers & AWS Fundamentals
summary: Cloud providers — AWS, GCP, Azure — are the infrastructure layer under every modern DevOps stack. AWS is the market leader. Understanding compute (EC2), storage (S3), networking (VPC, IAM), and managed Kubernetes (EKS) gives you a foundation that translates across all three clouds.

sections.title: Cloud computing models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
sections.body:
Cloud computing is one of the most important shifts in modern infrastructure — moving from owning physical hardware to renting capacity from a provider on demand. Understanding the service and deployment models is the foundation for every architecture decision you will make as a DevOps engineer.

**The shared responsibility model** is the first concept to internalise. Every cloud provider divides security and operational duties between what the provider handles and what you are responsible for. In IaaS, the provider manages the physical servers, networking switches, hypervisors, and data centre facilities; you are responsible for the operating system, runtime, application code, data, and identity management. In PaaS, the provider takes on more — the OS and runtime — leaving you responsible for the application and data. In SaaS, the provider manages everything and you simply configure and use the software. Knowing where the boundary lies determines what you must patch, audit, and protect.

**Elasticity** is what separates cloud from traditional hosting. Instead of buying servers for peak load and leaving them idle the rest of the time (CapEx), you pay for what you consume minute-by-minute (OpEx). A burst in traffic spins up more instances automatically; when traffic drops, instances terminate and billing stops. This model fundamentally changes how teams think about capacity planning.

**Regions and Availability Zones** are the building blocks of resilience. A region is a geographic cluster of data centres. Each region contains multiple Availability Zones (AZs) — physically isolated facilities within the same geographic area, connected by low-latency private fibre. Spreading your workload across AZs protects against a single facility failure. Spreading across regions protects against regional outages or serves globally distributed users with lower latency.

**Key terms you will encounter constantly:**

- **VPC (Virtual Private Cloud)** — your isolated private network inside the cloud, with full control over subnets, routing, and firewall rules
- **IAM (Identity and Access Management)** — the system controlling who or what can perform actions on cloud resources
- **Managed services** — cloud-provided components (databases, queues, caches) where the provider handles patching, backups, and scaling

Cloud providers rent you infrastructure on demand. You pay for what you use and scale in seconds instead of ordering servers.

**Service models:**

```
On-Premises  →  You manage everything (hardware, OS, runtime, app)
IaaS         →  Provider manages hardware; you manage OS up
PaaS         →  Provider manages OS + runtime; you manage app
SaaS         →  Provider manages everything; you use the software

Examples:
  IaaS:  AWS EC2, GCP Compute Engine, Azure VMs
  PaaS:  Heroku, AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Google App Engine
  SaaS:  GitHub, Datadog, Slack
```

**Deployment models:**

```
Public cloud   — infrastructure owned by provider, shared with others
               (AWS, GCP, Azure)

Private cloud  — infrastructure dedicated to one org
               (on-prem VMware, OpenStack)

Hybrid cloud   — mix of public and private
               (data on-prem, compute in cloud)

Multi-cloud    — using multiple public providers
               (AWS for compute, GCP for ML, Azure for M365 integration)
```

**Core cloud concepts:**

```
Region         — geographic area with multiple data centers
               (us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1)

Availability Zone (AZ) — isolated data center within a region
               (us-east-1a, us-east-1b, us-east-1c)
               Spread resources across AZs for high availability

Edge Location  — CDN endpoint, closer to users
               (CloudFront for AWS)

VPC            — Virtual Private Cloud: your isolated network

IAM            — Identity and Access Management: who can do what

Managed Service — provider runs the infrastructure component
               (RDS = managed Postgres, ElastiCache = managed Redis)
```

**Why cloud over on-prem?**
- No upfront hardware cost (OpEx vs CapEx)
- Horizontal scaling in seconds (autoscaling)
- Global availability without building data centers
- Managed services eliminate undifferentiated heavy lifting
- Pay-per-use: idle resources cost nothing if you terminate them

sections.title: IAM: identity, users, roles, and policies
sections.body:
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the security backbone of your AWS account. Every API call — whether from a human, a CI runner, or a running application — is authenticated and authorised through IAM. Getting IAM wrong is one of the most common causes of cloud security incidents, so understanding its model deeply is essential before you touch anything in production.

**Why IAM matters so much** is that AWS has no concept of a network perimeter the way a corporate data centre does. Any entity that holds valid credentials can call any AWS API from anywhere in the world. This makes strong IAM policies and the **principle of least privilege** — granting only the permissions required for a specific task, on specific resources, for a limited duration — the primary defence mechanism.

**The principal hierarchy** defines who or what performs actions. A **User** represents a person (or a CI system using static credentials — which is an anti-pattern for applications). A **Group** is a collection of users that share policies, making permission management easier at scale. A **Role** is the preferred mechanism for applications: it has no static credentials and instead issues temporary tokens that expire within hours. An EC2 instance, a Lambda function, a Kubernetes pod, or a CI runner can all assume roles to receive exactly the permissions they need, for exactly as long as they need them.

**IAM Policies** are JSON documents that explicitly allow or deny specific API actions on specific resources. The evaluation logic is: an explicit `Deny` always wins; without an explicit `Allow`, access is denied by default. This means you think about what you are permitting, not what you are blocking.

**ARNs (Amazon Resource Names)** are the universal identifiers for every AWS resource. Understanding the ARN format lets you write precise policies scoping permissions to exactly one bucket, one cluster, or one secret — not everything in the account.

**IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts)** is the Kubernetes-native mechanism for giving pods AWS access without hardcoded credentials. You annotate a Kubernetes ServiceAccount with an IAM role ARN; AWS and EKS use OIDC federation to issue temporary tokens to the pod automatically. Each pod can have a different, narrowly scoped role, and a compromise of one pod's credentials cannot be used to access a different service.

AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) controls who can do what in your AWS account. Getting IAM right is the foundation of cloud security.

**Core IAM objects:**

```
User         — a person or service with long-term credentials
               (avoid for applications — use roles instead)

Group        — collection of users sharing the same policies
               (Developers, Ops, ReadOnly)

Role         — a set of permissions that can be assumed
               (an EC2 instance assumes a role to call S3)
               No static credentials — uses temporary tokens

Policy       — JSON document defining allowed/denied actions
               Attached to users, groups, or roles
```

**Policy document anatomy:**

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "AllowS3ReadOnlyForBucket",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:GetObject",
        "s3:ListBucket"
      ],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:s3:::my-app-bucket",
        "arn:aws:s3:::my-app-bucket/*"
      ]
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyDeleteAnywhere",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "s3:DeleteObject",
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}
```

**IAM best practices:**

```
✗ Root account for daily use         → use it only for billing
✗ Long-term credentials for apps     → use IAM roles
✗ Wildcard actions (s3:*)            → scope to specific actions
✗ Sharing credentials                → one IAM user per person

✓ Enable MFA on root + all users
✓ Principle of least privilege: grant only what's needed
✓ Use IAM roles for EC2/Lambda/EKS
✓ Rotate access keys regularly
✓ Use AWS Organizations for multi-account structure
```

**Assume role (how apps get temporary credentials):**

```bash norun
# AWS CLI: assume a role and get temporary credentials
aws sts assume-role \
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/deploy-role \
  --role-session-name ci-deploy

# Output: AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, SessionToken (expire in 1h)

# In Kubernetes (IRSA: IAM Roles for Service Accounts)
# Pods in EKS can assume roles without static credentials
# annotation on ServiceAccount:
#   eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/my-role
```

**ARN format:**

```
arn:partition:service:region:account-id:resource
arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket              (no region/account for global services)
arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/admin   (no region for IAM)
arn:aws:ec2:us-east-1:123456789:instance/i-abc123
```

sections.title: Compute (EC2) and storage (S3, EBS)
sections.body:
EC2 and S3 are the two services that defined cloud computing. Almost everything else in AWS either builds on top of them or was designed to replace the need to manage them directly. Understanding how they work internally helps you choose the right instance type, storage class, and access pattern for your workloads.

**EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud)** provisions virtual machines called instances on multi-tenant hardware using the Nitro hypervisor. When you launch an instance you choose four things: the **AMI (Amazon Machine Image)** — a snapshot of an OS with pre-installed software; the **instance type** — how many vCPUs and how much RAM; the **network placement** — which VPC subnet and therefore which Availability Zone; and the **storage** — whether to use EBS volumes, instance store (ephemeral NVMe on the physical host), or EFS (shared network filesystem).

**Instance type naming** encodes useful information. The letter prefix denotes the family: `t` for burstable general-purpose, `m` for balanced, `c` for compute-optimised, `r` for memory-optimised, `g` for GPU. The number is the generation — higher is newer and usually better price/performance for the same size. The suffix is the size within the family.

**EBS (Elastic Block Store)** is a network-attached durable block device. Think of it as a hard drive that persists independently of the instance — you can detach it from one instance and attach it to another. The `gp3` type is the right default for most workloads: 3000 IOPS and 125 MB/s throughput included in the base price, with the ability to provision additional IOPS and throughput independently of capacity. Use `io2` for databases requiring very high, consistent IOPS.

**S3 (Simple Storage Service)** is fundamentally different from a filesystem. S3 stores objects — arbitrary blobs of data identified by a bucket name and a key (a path-like string). There is no real hierarchy; the `/` in a key is just a character that clients use to simulate folders. S3 guarantees **11 nines of durability** (99.999999999%) by storing data redundantly across at least three Availability Zones. S3 is also the backbone of Terraform remote state, static site hosting, and artifact storage in CI/CD pipelines.

**Storage classes** let you trade retrieval cost for storage cost. Data you access frequently belongs in Standard. Data you access a few times per month is cheaper in Standard-IA (Infrequent Access). Data you must keep for compliance but may never read again belongs in Glacier. S3 Intelligent-Tiering monitors access patterns and moves objects between tiers automatically.

## EC2: Elastic Compute Cloud

EC2 provides virtual machines (instances). You choose instance type, OS (AMI), network, and storage.

```bash norun
# List running instances
aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --filters Name=instance-state-name,Values=running \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,InstanceType,PublicIpAddress,Tags[?Key==`Name`].Value|[0]]' \
  --output table

# Launch an instance
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id ami-0c02fb55956c7d316 \
  --instance-type t3.micro \
  --key-name my-keypair \
  --security-group-ids sg-abc123 \
  --subnet-id subnet-abc123 \
  --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=web-server}]'

# SSH into instance
ssh -i ~/.ssh/my-keypair.pem ec2-user@<public-ip>

# Stop/terminate
aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-abc123
aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids i-abc123
```

**Instance types (naming convention):**

```
Family + Generation + Size

t3.micro    — burstable, cheapest, dev/test
t3.medium   — burstable, more memory
m6i.large   — general purpose, balanced
c6i.xlarge  — compute-optimized (web servers, batch)
r6i.2xlarge — memory-optimized (databases, caching)
g4dn.xlarge — GPU-optimized (ML inference)

Sizes: nano < micro < small < medium < large < xlarge < 2xlarge < ...
```

**EBS: Elastic Block Store** — persistent disk attached to EC2:

```bash norun
# Create a 50GB volume
aws ec2 create-volume \
  --availability-zone us-east-1a \
  --size 50 \
  --volume-type gp3

# Attach to an instance
aws ec2 attach-volume \
  --volume-id vol-abc123 \
  --instance-id i-abc123 \
  --device /dev/sdf

# Volume types:
# gp3 (SSD, general purpose) — default choice
# io2 (SSD, high IOPS)       — databases
# st1 (HDD, throughput)      — big data, sequential reads
# sc1 (HDD, cheapest)        — cold storage
```

## S3: Simple Storage Service

S3 is object storage — not a filesystem. Store any file as an object in a bucket. 99.999999999% durability.

```bash norun
# Create a bucket (must be globally unique)
aws s3 mb s3://my-app-artifacts-prod-2024

# Upload files
aws s3 cp build/app.tar.gz s3://my-app-artifacts-prod-2024/releases/v1.2.3/
aws s3 sync ./dist/ s3://my-static-site/  # sync directory

# List
aws s3 ls s3://my-app-artifacts-prod-2024/releases/

# Download
aws s3 cp s3://my-app-artifacts-prod-2024/releases/v1.2.3/app.tar.gz .

# Make object public (for static sites)
aws s3 website s3://my-static-site \
  --index-document index.html \
  --error-document error.html

# Presigned URL (temporary access without making public)
aws s3 presign s3://my-bucket/secret-file.pdf --expires-in 3600
```

**S3 storage classes (cost optimization):**

```
Standard         — frequently accessed, low latency
Intelligent-Tier — auto-moves between tiers based on access
Standard-IA      — infrequently accessed (lower cost, retrieval fee)
Glacier Instant  — archival, millisecond retrieval
Glacier Flexible — archival, minutes/hours retrieval, cheapest
```

sections.title: VPC: virtual private cloud and network design
sections.body:
The Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) is the network fabric inside which all your AWS resources live. Every EC2 instance, RDS database, EKS node, and Lambda function runs inside a VPC. Understanding VPC design is fundamental to security, performance, and connectivity — and it is one of the most common areas where teams make costly architectural mistakes early on.

**Why VPCs exist** is that the public cloud is shared infrastructure. Without network isolation, all resources across all customers would share a flat network. A VPC gives you a logically isolated section of the AWS network where you control the IP address space, subnets, routing tables, and firewalls. Resources inside your VPC are invisible to resources in other accounts unless you explicitly enable connectivity.

**The CIDR block** you assign to a VPC (e.g. `10.0.0.0/16`) defines the pool of private IP addresses available — 65,536 addresses in this case. You then divide this range into **subnets**, each tied to a specific Availability Zone. The critical design decision is **public vs private**: a public subnet has a route to an **Internet Gateway (IGW)**, making resources directly reachable from the internet; a private subnet has no direct internet route.

**The standard three-tier architecture** puts internet-facing load balancers and NAT Gateways in public subnets, application servers and Kubernetes nodes in private subnets, and databases in isolated private subnets with no outbound internet access at all. This limits the blast radius of a compromise — even if an attacker gains application-tier access, the database is not directly reachable from the internet.

**NAT Gateways** allow private-subnet resources to initiate outbound internet connections (to download packages, call external APIs) without being reachable inbound. The NAT Gateway lives in a public subnet and holds an Elastic IP; private subnets route `0.0.0.0/0` to the NAT Gateway.

**Security Groups** are stateful firewalls attached to individual resources. "Stateful" means that if you allow inbound port 443, the response traffic is automatically allowed outbound — no return rule needed. Security Groups can reference other Security Groups by ID, which is the correct pattern for allowing only app-tier instances to reach a database port.

**VPC Endpoints** are private connections from your VPC to AWS services (S3, DynamoDB, Secrets Manager) that bypass the internet entirely. Without them, a private-subnet EC2 calling S3 must route through a NAT Gateway, incurring extra cost and latency. With a VPC endpoint, traffic stays on the AWS private network.

A VPC is your isolated virtual network in AWS. Every resource (EC2, RDS, EKS) lives inside a VPC. Getting VPC design right is critical for security and connectivity.

```
VPC: 10.0.0.0/16  (65,536 IP addresses)
│
├── us-east-1a
│   ├── Public Subnet:  10.0.1.0/24   (internet-accessible)
│   │   └── NAT Gateway, Load Balancer, Bastion
│   └── Private Subnet: 10.0.11.0/24  (no direct internet)
│       └── EC2, RDS, EKS nodes
│
├── us-east-1b
│   ├── Public Subnet:  10.0.2.0/24
│   └── Private Subnet: 10.0.12.0/24
│
└── Internet Gateway (IGW) — connects public subnets to internet
```

**Key VPC components:**

```
Internet Gateway (IGW)  — allows public subnets to reach the internet
                          attach one IGW per VPC

NAT Gateway             — allows private subnets to initiate outbound
                          internet traffic (but not inbound)
                          sits in public subnet, used by private subnets

Route Table             — rules directing traffic (0.0.0.0/0 → IGW or NAT)

Security Group          — stateful firewall at instance level
                          allow inbound port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0

Network ACL (NACL)      — stateless firewall at subnet level
                          rarely configured manually

VPC Peering             — connect two VPCs (same or different accounts)

PrivateLink             — access AWS services without internet
                          (S3 VPC endpoint, no NAT Gateway needed)
```

**AWS CLI: inspect your VPC:**

```bash norun
# List VPCs
aws ec2 describe-vpcs --query 'Vpcs[*].[VpcId,CidrBlock,Tags[?Key==`Name`].Value|[0]]' --output table

# List subnets
aws ec2 describe-subnets \
  --query 'Subnets[*].[SubnetId,CidrBlock,AvailabilityZone,MapPublicIpOnLaunch]' \
  --output table

# List security groups and rules
aws ec2 describe-security-groups \
  --query 'SecurityGroups[*].[GroupId,GroupName,Description]' \
  --output table

# Check route tables
aws ec2 describe-route-tables \
  --query 'RouteTables[*].[RouteTableId,Routes[*].[DestinationCidrBlock,GatewayId]]' \
  --output table
```

**Security group vs NACL:**

```
                Security Group    Network ACL
Level           Instance          Subnet
State           Stateful          Stateless
Rules           Allow only        Allow + Deny
Evaluation      All rules         Numbered order
Default         Deny all in       Allow all
```

sections.title: EKS: Elastic Kubernetes Service
sections.body:
Amazon EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) is AWS's managed Kubernetes offering. Understanding what "managed" means precisely — what AWS handles versus what you remain responsible for — is essential before running production workloads on EKS.

**What AWS manages** is the Kubernetes control plane: the API server, the etcd datastore holding all cluster state, the controller manager, and the scheduler. AWS runs these components in a dedicated, isolated VPC that it manages, replicated across multiple Availability Zones. You pay approximately $0.10/hour for this guarantee. If the API server crashes, AWS restores it. If etcd has data corruption, AWS recovers it. You never SSH into the control plane.

**What you manage** is everything else: the worker nodes (EC2 instances running kubelet and the container runtime), the applications deployed on those nodes, network policies, RBAC configuration, and add-ons (networking CNI, storage drivers, ingress controllers). This is where most EKS operational complexity lives.

**Node groups** are the EC2 instances that run your pods. AWS-managed node groups handle AMI updates, cordon/drain, and instance replacement automatically — they are the right default. Fargate profiles provide serverless nodes where AWS provisions the underlying EC2 for each pod; useful for batch workloads where you want zero node management overhead.

**EKS networking** uses the AWS VPC CNI plugin, which allocates real VPC IP addresses to every pod directly from the subnet's IP range. This is different from most Kubernetes distributions that use an overlay network. The advantage is that AWS services (RDS, ElastiCache, API Gateway) see pod IPs as regular VPC traffic, simplifying security group rules. The tradeoff is that you must allocate sufficient IP address space in your subnets before cluster creation.

**IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts)** is the mechanism by which individual pods assume IAM roles without any static credentials. EKS establishes an OIDC identity provider; the AWS SDK inside a container uses a projected service account token to call AWS STS (Security Token Service) and receive temporary credentials scoped to the pod's IAM role. A compromise of one pod's temporary credentials cannot be used to access services that pod was not explicitly permitted to reach.

**EKS add-ons** are AWS-managed components installed into your cluster with version compatibility guaranteed. The VPC CNI, CoreDNS, and kube-proxy are required. The EBS CSI driver enables PersistentVolumes backed by EBS disks. The AWS Load Balancer Controller creates ALBs and NLBs from Ingress and Service resources — this replaces the need to provision load balancers manually.

EKS is AWS's managed Kubernetes. The control plane (API server, etcd) is managed by AWS; you manage the worker nodes (or use Fargate for serverless nodes).

**EKS architecture:**

```
AWS Account
│
├── EKS Control Plane (managed by AWS — you pay ~$0.10/hour)
│   ├── API Server
│   ├── etcd
│   └── Controller Manager
│
└── Your VPC
    ├── Node Group (EC2 instances running kubelet)
    │   ├── Worker Node (t3.large) — AZ a
    │   ├── Worker Node (t3.large) — AZ b
    │   └── Worker Node (t3.large) — AZ c
    └── Fargate Profile (optional: serverless pods)
```

**Create and connect to an EKS cluster:**

```bash norun
# eksctl is the recommended tool (wraps CloudFormation)
export CLUSTER_NAME=my-cluster
export REGION=us-east-1

# Create cluster (takes ~15 minutes)
eksctl create cluster \
  --name $CLUSTER_NAME \
  --region $REGION \
  --nodegroup-name standard-workers \
  --node-type t3.medium \
  --nodes 3 \
  --nodes-min 1 \
  --nodes-max 5 \
  --managed    # use managed node group (AWS handles AMI updates)

# Update kubeconfig
aws eks update-kubeconfig --name $CLUSTER_NAME --region $REGION
kubectl get nodes  # now talking to EKS

# Node groups
eksctl get nodegroup --cluster $CLUSTER_NAME
exsctl scale nodegroup --cluster $CLUSTER_NAME \
  --name standard-workers --nodes 5
```

**IRSA: IAM Roles for Service Accounts**

Instead of giving EC2 nodes broad IAM permissions, IRSA lets individual pods assume specific IAM roles:

```bash norun
# Enable IRSA on the cluster
eksctl utils associate-iam-oidc-provider \
  --cluster $CLUSTER_NAME --approve

# Create a service account with an IAM role
eksctl create iamserviceaccount \
  --name s3-reader \
  --namespace production \
  --cluster $CLUSTER_NAME \
  --attach-policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess \
  --approve
```

```yaml
# Pod uses the service account — gets S3 access without hardcoded keys
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: data-processor
spec:
  serviceAccountName: s3-reader
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: myapp:v1
    env:
    - name: AWS_REGION
      value: us-east-1
    # AWS SDK will auto-assume the role via IRSA
```

**EKS add-ons (managed by AWS):**

```bash norun
# List available add-ons
aws eks describe-addon-versions --region $REGION \
  --query 'addons[*].addonName' --output table

# Common add-ons:
# vpc-cni         — AWS VPC networking for pods
# coredns         — cluster DNS
# kube-proxy      — service routing
# aws-ebs-csi-driver — EBS persistent volumes
# aws-load-balancer-controller — ALB Ingress

# Install AWS Load Balancer Controller
export ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)
eksctl create iamserviceaccount \
  --cluster $CLUSTER_NAME \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --name aws-load-balancer-controller \
  --attach-policy-arn arn:aws:iam::$ACCOUNT_ID:policy/AWSLoadBalancerControllerIAMPolicy \
  --approve

helm repo add eks https://aws.github.io/eks-charts
helm install aws-load-balancer-controller eks/aws-load-balancer-controller \
  -n kube-system \
  --set clusterName=$CLUSTER_NAME \
  --set serviceAccount.create=false \
  --set serviceAccount.name=aws-load-balancer-controller
```

sections.title: Exercise: explore AWS concepts with the AWS CLI
sections.body:
Working with AWS from the command line is a daily DevOps activity. The AWS CLI's `--query` flag uses JMESPath expressions to filter and reshape JSON output, and the `--output table` flag turns results into a readable table. Mastering these two options means you can extract exactly the information you need without piping through `jq` or parsing raw JSON.

**Always check your identity** before running any AWS command (`aws sts get-caller-identity`). This simple habit prevents the painful mistake of running `terraform apply` against production when you meant staging — a mistake that happens far more often than teams admit.

**Tagging** is the operational backbone of a well-managed AWS account. Tags are key-value pairs attached to every resource. They power cost allocation (the bill broken down by team or environment), resource grouping, and access control (IAM policies can require or restrict access based on tags). A consistent tagging strategy — `Environment`, `Team`, `Application`, `ManagedBy` — should be enforced from the beginning via tag policies in AWS Organizations, not retrofitted later when you are trying to understand a surprise bill.

**Security auditing** with the CLI — scanning for security groups open to the world (`0.0.0.0/0` on sensitive ports), IAM users without MFA, public S3 buckets — is a routine task you will perform or automate. The `--query` syntax makes these one-liners possible without installing additional tools.

**Cost awareness** must be built in from day one. Cloud resources billed hourly or per-GB add up quickly. Set a billing alarm (`aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm`) that triggers when your account crosses a threshold, and use `aws ce get-cost-and-usage` in scripts or dashboards to track spending over time.

In the **local sandbox**, `kubectl` speaks to a k3s cluster that behaves identically to EKS from an application perspective: the same Kubernetes API, the same resource types, the same RBAC model. The key difference is that k3s runs the control plane as a single process inside Docker rather than as a managed multi-AZ service, but for learning Kubernetes operations, it is fully equivalent.

The sandbox doesn't have AWS credentials, but the concepts and CLI patterns below are exactly what you'll use with a real AWS account. Run these commands against a real account or study the expected output.

```bash norun
# ── Install/configure AWS CLI ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# Check if available in the sandbox terminal:
aws --version

# Configure with credentials (for real AWS accounts):
# aws configure
# → AWS Access Key ID:
# → AWS Secret Access Key:
# → Default region: us-east-1
# → Default output format: json

# ── Query patterns you'll use daily ───────────────────────────────────────

# 1. List running EC2 instances in table format
aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --filters Name=instance-state-name,Values=running \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,InstanceType,State.Name,PublicIpAddress]' \
  --output table

# 2. List S3 buckets and their sizes
aws s3 ls
aws s3 ls s3://my-bucket --recursive --human-readable --summarize

# 3. Check your identity
aws sts get-caller-identity

# 4. List IAM roles
aws iam list-roles \
  --query 'Roles[*].[RoleName,Arn,CreateDate]' \
  --output table

# 5. Get all resources with a specific tag
aws resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources \
  --tag-filters Key=Environment,Values=production \
```
